An appeal ending early does not waive the rest of its admission window. An already-started ordinary round is not cancelled by this hold; this does not permit admitting a second ordinary round for the same item and pool.

If a nonempty ordinary jury draw completed before final accuracy closure or completion of an otherwise permitted voluntary author withdrawal, that already-drawn attempt continues against its pinned revision and policy. The exit does not discard votes, shorten commitment, reveal or proof-opening deadlines, release its active collateral or jury-fee reservation, or waive ordinary participation and coherence rules. Protocol execution order determines whether the completed draw preceded the exit; scheduled preparation, an incomplete draw or an empty draw does not qualify for this continuation permission.

A valid ruling from that surviving attempt earns the normal ETH service fee and opens its normal first appeal admission and funding windows, even though the item is inactive. The earlier exit is not replayed to cancel this newly opened process merely because no positions were funded before the exit. Its subsequent zero-funded, unopposed and contested outcomes, fees, appeals and settlement follow the common rules. This is a specific permission for the appeal chain originating from the already-drawn attempt, not permission for unrelated chains or later independent ordinary rounds. All resulting scores remain historical assessments of the pinned revision: neither the ordinary ruling nor a later relevance outcome restores active status, feed eligibility, beneficiary funding or a returned author bond. Authorship alone does not make the author a party. Withdrawal eligibility and timing remain unchanged.

If that ordinary attempt fails quorum, it completes the ordinary proof-opening and failure-settlement rules without a new score, ETH fee or appeal window. Settle its utility-token collateral and penalties normally, and return only its unused ordinary jury-fee reservation through the existing cancellation path. Existing historical scores and previously earned entitlements remain unchanged. No fresh ordinary retry may be drawn for the inactive item, even if the application's ordinary retry allowance has not been exhausted. This does not cancel a retry whose own nonempty draw already completed before the exit: that attempt qualifies under the same drawn-jury continuation rule. Still-active items retain their ordinary retry rules, and protected appeal chains retain their separate retry rules.

The following appeal-continuation and cancellation rules apply both when a separate accuracy decision finally closes or debunks an item and when an otherwise permitted voluntary author withdrawal completes. A withdrawal request or an unfinished cooldown alone does not trigger these rules. Withdrawal eligibility, cooldowns, author-bond return and the application's existing status and funding consequences remain unchanged; a relevance appeal does not add a wait for chain finality to an otherwise permitted withdrawal. This provision creates no withdrawal right in an application that does not already permit one.

If at least one level of the same ongoing relevance-appeal chain became contested through two or more fully funded distinct positions before either event, that existing funded chain continues under its agreed rules. This applies even when a later level in the same chain is still admitting or funding proposals at the time of closure or completed withdrawal. The pinned revision and policy, score proposals, deadlines, reservations, jury rules and fee terms remain in force. Neither event cancels an in-progress appeal jury, stops its quorum retries, shortens its admission or funding window, or prevents further appeals of rulings in that same chain using fresh funding under the existing rules. No party is compelled to fund a further level, and the ordinary zero-funded, unopposed and contested outcomes still determine how that chain proceeds and ends.

For a chain protected by prior contested funding, neither event forces a zero relevance score, creates early finality, refunds accepted contributions or releases reserved fees. The chain's own terminal score determines its backer settlements, including earlier adjudicated pots; earned jury fees remain earned, and additional valid appeal rulings incur only their normally defined fees. Failed-quorum attempts remain fee-free under the existing rule. This preserves the funded contest even though continued adjudication may cost ETH and repeated appeals or failed quorum can prolong the capital lock.

Accuracy closure and completed withdrawal retain their respective effects on feed eligibility, confidence and beneficiary funding under the applicable policy. A later relevance ruling is recorded for the historical item's pinned revision and settles the existing contest; it cannot reopen the item, restore feed eligibility or restart beneficiary funding. Apart from the first appeal process arising from the surviving ordinary attempt described above, this continuation rule does not authorize new ordinary rounds or unrelated appeal chains for an item closed or withdrawn under its existing rules. If either event instead becomes effective while the initial appeal process is still open and no level in that same chain has ever had two fully funded distinct positions, cancel that initial appeal process. Stop proposal admission and contributions immediately, without waiting for the scheduled cutoffs. The already-issued relevance score remains the terminal score; no proposed score wins by forfeiture, no zero score is substituted, and no appeal jury or appeal jury fee is created. Every accepted contribution becomes refundable in full, including contributions to a lone fully funded position. Refunds use the existing permissionless collection and standing receiving-address rules and do not undergo payout rounding. They become claimable at that event without waiting for another contributor to collect.

Before applying this cancellation, respect any finality already established under the existing deadlines or outcome rules. A completed or logically final chain is not reopened merely because its finality has not yet been recorded by a later transaction. In particular, a forfeiture score that became final before either event remains final. This cancellation is a specific exception to the initial admission and funding windows, not a general power to alter their duration. It ends only this process's hold; other holds and the item's resulting ordinary eligibility restrictions remain in force.

At the effective accuracy-closure or completed-withdrawal transition, the decision between cancellation and protected continuation must use one atomic view of that chain's funding history. A valid contribution that completes the second distinct position before that event protects the funded chain, even if its jury has not yet started. If the event occurs first while no contested level has ever funded, later proposals and contributions are rejected and cannot revive the process. Existing deadline validation still applies to the contribution; signing or broadcasting earlier does not make an otherwise late contribution eligible.

Only unused reservations belonging to the cancelled appeal process are unwound. Return any unused pool reservation to that pool; keep accepted contributions reserved for their backers' refunds rather than crediting them to the pool or releasing them twice. Other groups' reserves remain untouched. The cancellation does not reclaim or repay already-earned jury fees, including unpaid fees still assigned to their recipients. No earlier contested pot exists in this branch. An author who also backs a position remains subject to these same backer rules; returning the author bond does not by itself release separately committed appeal funds. For example, with a target of 100 per position, contributions of 100 and 90 before either event become refunds of 100 and 90. If both positions reached 100 before the event, the funded-chain continuation rule applies instead.

For pools with recurring ordinary reassessment, let $t_{\mathrm{clear}}$ be the protocol timestamp at which the last applicable admission window or active appeal stops holding the item, and let $\Delta_{\mathrm{ordinary}}$ be the pool's ordinary cadence. The next ordinary round becomes eligible at $t_{\mathrm{clear}}+\Delta_{\mathrm{ordinary}}$, after one full cadence. For example, if a weekly round was due on day 7 but the last hold ends on day 10, its next eligibility is day 17. The old calendar phase and missed occurrences do not create a catch-up backlog; a previously due but unstarted round cannot begin before the new eligibility time. Eligibility still requires the ordinary item, funding and scheduling conditions and does not guarantee execution at that timestamp. If another applicable hold begins before the round starts, it blocks that start; the next eligibility is recomputed from the end of the last such hold. Ending one group while another hold remains does not start the interval. The anchor is the protocol's hold-end time, not when a scheduler notices it or someone records closure or collects a refund or payout. This timing rule does not cancel an already-started ordinary round, permit overlapping ordinary rounds, delay an appeal jury or change failed-appeal retry timing. Later ordinary rounds do not reopen completed appeal settlements.

A shared-jury attempt that fails the 80% reveal-weight quorum is cancelled without a new score, jury fee or curator reward subsidy. The contested level remains active and retries at the existing cadence without a retry-count limit or elapsed-time cancellation. Each retry uses its own completed draw for quorum coverage but retains the level's recorded positions, contribution target, planned jury size, pay rate, fee ceiling and funding reservations. It neither reopens funding nor requires top-ups. Existing non-participation penalties, leak-report transfers and release of valid participants' round locks still apply. Accepted contributions and fee reserves stay unavailable for reuse; failed quorum neither spends nor releases them. The previous effective score and ordinary-round hold persist.

#### Common-pot fee accounting

Fresh eligible jury-fee reservations use a pool's unencumbered ETH service budget in successful protocol execution order. Each commitment atomically reads the available balance and reserves the amount permitted by its funding rule. The first successful commitment therefore takes precedence over a later one, including at the same timestamp. Earlier filing, becoming ready, an ordinary round becoming due, signing or broadcasting does not itself reserve funds. Rejected or ineligible attempts acquire no reservation. Existing reservations, earned but unclaimed fees, accepted backer contributions and funds committed to other obligations cannot be counted as available service-budget ETH or taken by a later round. Pools do not compete for one another's funds.

This rule governs competition between fresh appeal commitments and otherwise eligible ordinary commitments; it does not override the application's order among ordinary rounds or any round's eligibility, scheduling and funding conditions. In particular, it does not let an appeal reserve early while admission or unresolved funding outcomes still require it to wait. Ordinary rounds retain their existing full-reservation requirement. An eligible appeal instead uses available pool funding and reserves the shortfall from its own common pot without waiting for the pool to replenish. A commitment keeps its recorded funding split: later deposits or returned reserves become available to later commitments, not a retroactive subsidy for an earlier one. Existing appeal retries retain their original reservations and do not compete again. Releases continue to follow the existing issuance or cancellation rules.

For example, two eligible appeals for different items in the same pool each have two positions contributing 0.20 ETH and each earn a jury fee of 0.10 ETH. With only 0.10 ETH unencumbered in the service budget, the first reservation funds its fee from the pool and leaves 0.40 ETH in its backer pot. The second funds its fee from its own pot and leaves 0.30 ETH. Both appeals proceed. Execution order determines the subsidy recipient; it is not a fairness guarantee. Faster inclusion can obtain the subsidy, and an appeal can consume funds before an ordinary round reserves them, leaving that ordinary round awaiting funding.

For a contested group of $m\ge2$ fully funded positions with distinct recorded scores, each position contributes $C$ to a common pot of $mC$. Let $B\ge0$ be the unencumbered ETH service-budget balance recorded at this successful fee commitment. Before drawing or seating the jury, reserve $U_{\max}=\min(B,J_{\max})$ from the pool and $D_{\max}=J_{\max}-U_{\max}$ from the common pot. The same money cannot support another reservation or payout. A pool shortfall does not impose a replenishment wait: the contest funds cover it under the frozen ceiling.

At valid-ruling issuance, charge the earned fee $J$ to the pool as $U=\min(B,J)$ and to the contest only as $D=J-U$, once. The resulting juror fee entitlements are immediately withdrawable under the Relevance layer's rule, even while the remaining backer pot stays locked. Unclaimed service fees, including fees redirected to successful leak reporters, remain committed to their assigned recipients; later collection must not charge the pool or contest again. The unused pool reserve $U_{\max}-U$ returns to the pool. The contest's unused reserve $D_{\max}-D$ stays in its locked funds until chain finality. Releasing a pool reserve does not release the backers' capital. A later appeal jury has its own fee commitment and cannot charge this earlier contest. The net settlement pot is

$$
Q=mC-D>0.
$$

Since $0\le D\le J\le J_{\max}<2C\le mC$, this pot stays positive even when the pool contributes nothing. The single fee shortfall reduces the common pot once, regardless of how many positions fund. The ceiling is binding; unused capacity cannot be charged as a fee. With no contested jury, no jury fee is incurred. For example, three positions contributing 200 each create a gross pot of 600; an actual fee of 100 with no pool contribution leaves 500 for eventual distribution. The inverse-distance rule below determines each included position's share at chain finality.

#### Inverse-distance scalar payout

Let $s_i$ be position $i$'s fixed proposed score and $r$ the ultimate final score of the same appeal chain. Define its absolute distance as $e_i=|s_i-r|$. When every included position has $e_i>0$, its ideal total payout, including any returned principal, is

$$
P_i^*=Q\frac{1/e_i}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}1/e_j}.
$$

The ideal payouts sum to the net common pot $Q$. Every positive-distance position has a positive ideal share. A closer position has a larger ideal share; halving the distance doubles its ideal payout relative to a position whose distance is unchanged. Adding another positive-distance position changes the common pot and normalization, but not the ratio between two existing positive-distance ideal payouts at a fixed terminal score. These comparisons precede integer rounding and do not establish neutrality to additional proposals or a truthful-reporting incentive.

If exactly one included position has $e_i=0$, its ideal payout is all of $Q$ and the others' ideal payouts are zero. This explicit exact-match branch agrees with the limit as that position's distance tends to zero while the others remain positive; no positive tolerance is substituted for zero. The one-position-per-score rule permits at most one exact-match position for this ruling. Its backers share that position's payout through their contribution records; supporting the same exact score does not create another winning position.

Express $Q$ and all ETH payouts in integer wei. Each position's payable allocation is the floor of its ideal share:

$$
P_i=\lfloor P_i^*\rfloor,\qquad
d_{\mathrm{dust}}=Q-\sum_{i=1}^{m}P_i.
$$

At chain finality, credit the rounding remainder $d_{\mathrm{dust}}$ exactly once to the same pool's ETH jury-service budget and reserve each $P_i$ for that position's backers. The accounting identity is $Q=\sum_iP_i+d_{\mathrm{dust}}$. Since $d_{\mathrm{dust}}$ is an integer sum of $m$ fractional parts, $0\le d_{\mathrm{dust}}\le m-1$; the proposal grid therefore bounds it by 100 wei per adjudicated level. The exact-match branch has $d_{\mathrm{dust}}=0$. This bound requires the floor of the intended ideal share, without extra losses from intermediate truncation or approximate reciprocal weights. Positive ideal shares can round to zero, and unequal ideal shares can round to the same integer. Unclaimed allocations remain assigned to their backers; they are not rounding remainders and cannot be swept into the service budget. This credit neither changes an already earned jury fee nor reuses a reserved balance.

Each position distributes its whole-wei allocation among its accepted contributions using the cumulative rule below. It leaves no second backer-level remainder for the pool. A closer position can still lose principal after fees. Target and other fee rounding remain to be specified.

For exactly two opposing positions A and B with distinct proposed scores $a$ and $b$, the rule reduces to the established comparison

$$
P_A^*=Q\frac{e_B}{e_A+e_B},\qquad
P_B^*=Q\frac{e_A}{e_A+e_B}.
$$

Equal positive distances give equal ideal payouts and equal floored allocations. Distinct opposing scores ensure $e_A+e_B\ge|a-b|>0$ in this two-position form. Neither position is required to be the previous ruling's score, and the jury may issue a score different from every proposal.

With three positions at 0.20, 0.60 and 0.90 and a terminal score of 0.70, distances are 0.50, 0.10 and 0.20. Their reciprocal weights are 2, 10 and 5. A net pot of 500 has ideal payouts $1000/17$, $5000/17$ and $2500/17$, approximately 58.82, 294.12 and 147.06 before asset-unit rounding. If this illustrative pot is 500 wei, the payable allocations are 58, 294 and 147 wei, and the pool's ETH jury-service budget receives the remaining 1 wei at chain finality. These are total allocations, not profits.

For example, $a=0.80$, $b=0.20$ and terminal score $r=0.70$ produce a 5:1 ratio of ideal shares. With 100 contributed to each position and no fee charged to the contest, the ideal payouts are $166\tfrac{2}{3}$ and $33\tfrac{1}{3}$. A fee deduction of 20 leaves a pot of 180 and payouts of 150 and 30. If an intermediate score is 0.70 but the ultimate final score is 0.30, that same net pot instead pays 30 and 150; the intermediate calculation was never claimable. Neither position is required to be the previous ruling's score, and the jury may issue a score different from both proposals.

Under the default multiplier, a maximum fee of 100 requires 200 from each of two positions. With no pool contribution and an actual fee of 100, $Q=300$. A unique exact prediction earns 300 on its position's 200 contribution. This does not guarantee profit for a closer but inexact prediction or establish an optimal multiplier.

#### Cumulative allocation to backers

Within a fully funded position $i$, number its positive accepted contributions in the order they are applied to the protocol's state. Let $c_{i,\ell}$ be contribution $\ell$ in integer wei, and define cumulative accepted funding by $F_{i,0}=0$ and $F_{i,\ell}=F_{i,\ell-1}+c_{i,\ell}$. The final cumulative amount equals the frozen position target $C>0$. Acceptance must atomically fix each contribution's amount, recorded backer and interval $[F_{i,\ell-1},F_{i,\ell})$ together with the funded balance. A timestamp alone does not determine this order. Rejected offers, excess above the cap and zero accepted amounts create no interval. Multiple accepted contributions from the same backer retain separate intervals; later contributions or claims cannot reorder or merge the intervals used for allocation.

Once the chain is final and position allocation $P_i$ is fixed, the contribution's payable entitlement is

$$
A_{i,\ell}=
\left\lfloor\frac{P_iF_{i,\ell}}{C}\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor\frac{P_iF_{i,\ell-1}}{C}\right\rfloor.
$$

The recorded backer's total is the sum over its contributions. Evaluate each product and quotient with exact floor semantics; intermediate overflow or early truncation must not change the mathematical result. Claims may arrive in any order without changing allocations, and a contribution's entitlement may be collected at most once. The amount is claimable under the existing chain-finality rule and the permissionless collection rule below; aggregation and the remaining transfer mechanics remain to be specified. Computing one contribution's entitlement requires no ranking or traversal of other backers, but collecting an address's many contributions is not thereby guaranteed a bounded cost.

The interval allocations telescope to $P_i$, including when $P_i=0$, so all of the position's allocation remains assigned to its backers. There is no backer-rounding residue to credit to the pool. An unclaimed entitlement remains reserved; it is not reassigned to the last claimant or swept into the jury-service budget. This rule applies to adjudicated payouts only. Full-principal refunds for underfunded or unopposed positions still return each accepted contribution $c_{i,\ell}$ exactly.

For four contributions of 1 wei to a target of 4 wei, a position payout of 2 wei produces entitlements of 0, 1, 0 and 1 wei in acceptance order. Each contribution's entitlement differs from its ideal proportional amount $P_i c_{i,\ell}/C$ by less than 1 wei, because its error is the difference between two rounding errors. Splitting a contribution into adjacent intervals leaves its combined entitlement unchanged. This is a per-contribution bound, not a bound per backer or economic actor. Interleaving contributions can change the allocation: with ten 1-wei contributions sharing 3 wei, the fourth, seventh and tenth contributions receive 1 wei each. An actor occupying those three intervals receives 3 wei despite supplying only three-tenths of the funding. Rounding differences can accumulate across many contributions. This conditional example does not establish a profitable strategy, and the rule does not establish neutrality to funding order or identity splitting.

#### Permissionless collection of internal ETH entitlements

Each original recorded recipient has one standing receiving-address setting in each paying contract for its internal ETH jury-service fees, appeal payouts and contribution refunds. This includes fees assigned to a successful leak reporter. The setting defaults to the original recipient. Only that original recipient may change the receiving address or reset it to itself. A change applies to all its unpaid entitlements in this scope, including amounts accrued before the change, and to future entitlements from that paying contract. It remains effective until another authorized change; no approval per payment is required.

The original recipient remains the entitlement owner. The receiving address gains no right to change the setting or to authorize another receiver merely by receiving funds. A caller, funder or protocol operator cannot change it on the recipient's behalf without valid authorization. For a contract recipient, the authority must come from that contract through its own supported mechanism, not from an assumed human controller. If the original recipient cannot authorize an update, appointing a receiving address does not create a recovery administrator or restore that lost authority.

Once an entitlement is claimable, anyone may trigger payment to the original recipient's current receiving address without a separate recipient signature or participation role. The caller cannot choose a different destination, change the amount or advance eligibility, and receives no reward or reimbursement entitlement from triggering. Existing records determine ownership and amount; the existing issuance, finality or refund rule determines claimability. The original recipient and its current receiving address may also trigger collection. No automatic payment is required, and collection is not a prerequisite for issuance, finality or another claimant's eligibility.

Resolve the receiving address from current authorized state when each payment executes, rather than fixing it at accrual or accepting a caller's stale destination instruction. The setting lookup, transfer and successful entitlement settlement must behave as one atomic operation. If a payment executes before a receiving-address update, it uses the then-current address and remains final. If the update executes first, a subsequent payment must use the new address. Broadcast or signing time does not override execution order. Completed payments are not reopened or clawed back by a later update. There is no parallel per-payment authorization route that can bypass the current setting.

A successful transfer satisfies the same entitlement once, regardless of the caller or current receiving address. Collection cannot charge the original funding source again, modify another owner's entitlement or reuse an already-paid amount. A failed transfer leaves the unpaid entitlement and its reserve intact and retryable; it does not count as collection. Unclaimed balances remain reserved under their existing accounting rules. Changing the receiving address does not itself pay a claim, require an earlier failed transfer, create a fresh balance or release a reserve.

Receiving-address updates must be authenticated as instructions of the original recipient and valid for the relevant chain and paying contract. If signed update instructions are supported, their validation must prevent forgery, cross-deployment reuse and a superseded instruction restoring an old address after a later authorized update. The update interface, credential format and replay-protection representation remain implementation work; no signature scheme is selected here. Transfer-failure isolation and batching also remain to be specified. This rule does not extend to author bonds, beneficiary-registry payments, utility-token rewards or utility-stake withdrawals.

The unresolved specification includes non-default multiplier calibration, proof validation, payout-claim mechanics, target and other fee rounding, and other cancellation outcomes. The execution priority and reservation of ordinary penalties relative to same-round leak confiscation also remain unspecified: the original-weight penalty formulas and capped leak transfer must not spend the same collateral twice. Selecting the reference per-seat rate does not resolve its empirical adequacy or joint calibration with utility-token exposure. These choices are not established by the inverse-distance formula.

The proposal grid prevents arbitrarily close distinct positions, but adjacent values such as 0.59 and 0.60 can still be funded separately. It does not establish neutrality to additional positions or resistance to capital concentration. Crowdfunding can assemble capital from several backers, but opposition still needs sufficient funding in time. An unopposed proposal can prevail by forfeiture independently of its merits. A bounded admission window gives later contributors a predictable opportunity to enter; it does not establish truthful reporting or independent judgment. Neither sufficient funds nor a larger jury guarantees correction. Stake determines influence and exposure, not expertise or distinct identity.

## Confidence

Confidence is not a truth label. It is accumulated bond-time. Let $C$ denote the resulting confidence score, let $B_t$ denote the bond active during interval $\Delta t$, and let the summation run over the item's bonded history:

$$
C = \sum_t B_t \cdot \Delta t
$$

The semantics are simple:

- larger bond means more capital at risk
- longer survival means longer exposure to challenge
- challenge pauses accumulation; a successful defense resumes accrual from the paused integral
- amendment (`PendingEdit -> Live`) resets confidence to zero, since the content has changed
- withdrawal freezes the score permanently

An interface may use confidence for ranking or display, but it must not conflate confidence with a universal truth claim. Confidence measures accumulated capital exposure over time, not community validation or endorsement. A failed challenge supplies evidence about the challenged proposition only to the extent that the evidence and adjudication were reliable; it does not validate every proposition in the item. Bond-time can grow without scrutiny. @fig-confidence-reputation illustrates the accounting dynamics.

There is therefore no protocol-level dollar cutoff at which a claim becomes "noise." Confidence is continuous. A low bond supplies little capital exposure; whether it deters deception depends on the benefit of surviving falsehood and the detection and adjudication probabilities in Claim 1. Interfaces may impose visibility thresholds, but those thresholds are product policy rather than validated protocol constants.

## Reputation

The current design uses a single reputation system:

- **Author reputation** is a pool-scoped, slowly decaying credibility stock. It is not escrowed per claim, but every new claim exposes the author's standing reputation to large downside if the claim is debunked. Reputation gains follow a final `ChallengeFailed` ruling, not survival without a challenge; decay follows calendar epochs. A reputation update caused by one claim does not affect the confidence or relevance of the author's other claims; each claim continues under its own bond-time history.

The design deliberately avoids any reputation-weighted mechanism for curation. An earlier iteration allowed reputation to directly increase curation weight; the current design rejects that entirely because it grants influence not fully backed by slashable capital. Curation drafting and voting are both purely stake-driven.

![Schematic accounting trajectories, not numerical executions of the protocol rules. Confidence accumulates bond-time while a claim is live, pauses during challenges, and freezes at withdrawal. Reputation rises after favorable adjudication and falls on debunking; the right panel illustrates different frequencies of adverse outcomes, not a demonstrated separation by author type.](diagrams/fig-confidence-reputation.png){#fig-confidence-reputation}

## Local pool economics

Each pool has its own ETH service budget (@fig-pool-economics), separate from utility-token deposits and penalty balances. The pool creator or any sponsor can top it up. Ordinary scheduled relevance-round service fees are paid from that local ETH budget. If it runs dry, those scheduled rounds pause; the canonical record remains challengeable. For contested appeals, available pool funds pay first and contest funds cover only the shared-jury fee shortfall under [Public appeal funding](#sec-appeal-funding). Two funded positions provide more than the frozen maximum fee, so a depleted pool does not impose a replenishment wait. The shortfall is charged once to their common pot. The remaining pot follows the inverse-distance payout rule at chain finality.

Challenge tax is paid by the challenger and routed to the challenged pool's reward budget. For immediately active challenges, the tax credits at filing; for queued challenges, the tax remains in escrow until activation and is refunded if the challenge is cancelled or mooted by an earlier debunking. On a failed challenge, the pool-budget share of the challenger's counter-stake (determined by the pool's payout-split ratio) also credits the pool. Both inflows are dispute-dependent: a peaceful pool generates zero endogenous revenue. This makes pool economics local rather than governance-allocated, but also makes peacetime ordinary-round funding entirely sponsor-dependent.

![Pool economics money flow for ETH. The service budget is funded by pool creators and challenge taxes, and pays relevance-round service fees to curators. Utility-token deposits and penalties are separate and not shown. Challenger counter-stakes flow through dispute resolution independently.](diagrams/fig-pool-economics.png){#fig-pool-economics}

# Equilibrium Analysis

This section examines how private returns could support the intended public outcome, deriving participation thresholds in simplified expected-value models and testing a truthful-reporting claim. The labeled claims are not formal theorems with full proofs. Claim 3 identifies a unilateral reward increase in a single-asset analytical model; it does not calculate two-asset payoffs or net returns after appeals. The participation conditions do not establish equilibrium.

## Author's strategy

An author who publishes a false claim derives value $V$ if the claim survives (attention, reputational gain, advertising revenue from a false ad). The author posts bond $B$. Let $p_{\text{detect}}$ denote the probability that the false claim is detected and challenged in the modeled window, and let $P_{\text{maj}}(p, N)$ denote majority correctness for an odd-sized jury of $N$ independent jurors, each correct with probability $p$. The expected value (EV) of publishing a false claim is:

$$
\text{EV}_{\text{false author}} = (1 - p_{\text{detect}} \cdot P_{\text{maj}}) \cdot V - p_{\text{detect}} \cdot P_{\text{maj}} \cdot B
$$

Setting $\text{EV}_{\text{false author}} < 0$ and solving for $B$ yields a bond threshold $B^*$ above which false publication has negative expected value:

$$
B^* = V \cdot \frac{1 - p_{\text{detect}} \cdot P_{\text{maj}}}{p_{\text{detect}} \cdot P_{\text{maj}}}
$$

**Claim 1.** *When $p_{\text{detect}}P_{\text{maj}}>0$, false publication has negative expected value in this model if $B>B^*$. Holding jury quality fixed at $P_{\text{maj}}(0.80, 5) \approx 0.94$, $B^*/V$ falls from roughly $20$ at $p_{\text{detect}}=0.05$ to $9.6$ at $0.10$, $2.0$ at $0.35$, $1.1$ at $0.50$, and $0.3$ at $0.80$. If detection or correct adjudication has zero probability, no finite bond deters a positive benefit $V$. The reference point ($p_{\text{detect}}=0.35$, $B^* \approx 2.0V$) is illustrative, not a calibrated prediction.*

This comparison is against abstention with zero payoff. It omits publication costs, capital opportunity costs, and author rewards from failed challenges. It does not establish a preference for honest publication, whose payoff is not modeled, or deter attackers whose external benefits exceed the assumed $V$.

Within this model, a bond below $B^*$ does not deter the assumed deception. Accumulated bond-time does not change that instantaneous deterrence threshold.

This paper does not estimate $p_{\text{detect}}$ empirically. Rather than arguing for a single point value, we report the deterrence threshold as a function of detection coverage across the range $p_{\text{detect}} \in [0.05, 0.80]$, holding jury quality fixed at $p=0.80$ and $N=5$. The threshold is first-order sensitive to this parameter: $B^*/V \approx 20$ at $p_{\text{detect}}=0.05$, $9.6$ at $0.10$, $4.3$ at $0.20$, $2.0$ at $0.35$, $1.1$ at $0.50$, and $0.3$ at $0.80$ (see @fig-e1-detect-sensitivity). Detection coverage is therefore a first-order viability condition for the accuracy layer, not a secondary nuisance parameter. The $p_{\text{detect}}=0.35$ anchor used elsewhere in the paper sits near the middle of this range and serves as an illustrative reference point, not a calibrated forecast.

## Challenger's entry decision

A challenger does not arrive with a known false claim. They must search. Let $e$ denote the effort cost of examining one claim, let $\beta$ denote the base rate of false claims in the pool, let $p_{\text{detect|examined}}$ denote the probability that examination reveals falsity, and let $\text{EV}_{\text{false}}$ denote the challenger's expected value on a known false claim from the accuracy layer. The expected value of examining one claim is:

$$
\text{EV}_{\text{search}} = \beta \cdot p_{\text{detect|examined}} \cdot \text{EV}_{\text{false}} - e
$$

Searching is profitable when:

$$
\beta > \beta^* = \frac{e}{p_{\text{detect|examined}} \cdot \text{EV}_{\text{false}}}
$$

**Claim 2.** *For a challenger with the specified costs, $p_{\text{detect|examined}}>0$ and $\text{EV}_{\text{false}}>0$, search has positive expected value when $\beta>\beta^*$. Below that threshold, this model favors abstention. Heterogeneous costs, private information, or external rewards can support search outside that condition. Low search activity can reflect either few false claims or inadequate incentives to detect them; it is not evidence of accuracy.*

The free-rider dimension compounds this problem [@groves1977freeriderproblem]. A challenger who debunks a false claim can benefit all readers while bearing search costs privately. Challenge rewards provide a private return, but whether they induce adequate search depends on costs, competing investigators, and detection coverage. The model does not solve that strategic entry problem.

## Curator voting strategy

The coherence game asks curators to report relevance scores in $[0, 1]$. On-chain commitments conceal reports until revelation; they do not prevent private disclosure or prior coordination. The model assumes each curator $i$ has a private signal $\theta_i$ about the policy-implied relevance $r$ and forms a belief about the distribution of others' signals. Here $r$ denotes the latent relevance value implied by the pool policy, $\theta_i$ denotes curator $i$'s noisy private estimate of that value, and $K$ is the coherence-threshold multiplier from the slashing rule. The collusion sweeps describe outcomes at selected stake fractions; they do not estimate an equilibrium or incentive-compatibility threshold.

**Claim 3 (single-asset model).** *A dispersion-scaled single-asset reward can permit a unilateral report to increase the reporter's payout without distance-based slashing. This is not a payoff result for the two-asset design, which pays a fixed ETH fee per timely, validly revealed seat.*

Consider an analytical model with base reward $R$, minimum reward fraction $\rho\in[0,1]$, and positive reference dispersion $\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}$. It distributes $f_{\mathrm{reward}}R$ among coherent revealers in proportion to locked weight, where

$$
f_{\mathrm{reward}}=\rho+(1-\rho)\min(1,\sigma/\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}).
$$

For 15 equal-weight curators who all observe $r=0.5$ without noise, set $K=1.25$, $\varepsilon_\sigma=\sigma_{\mathrm{ref}}=0.02$, $\rho=0.1$, and an illustrative $R=0.01$ ETH. All reports of $0.5$ give each curator $0.000066667$ ETH. One report of $0.51$ instead gives $\mu=0.5006667$ and $\sigma\approx0.00249444$, still below the dispersion floor, and increases every curator's modeled reward, including the deviator's, to approximately $0.000141500$ ETH. These numbers follow from that single-asset formula; they are not rewards under the selected two-asset rule. Commit-reveal does not prevent the preplanned report. Contributions, counterparty awards, service costs and later penalties are absent from the calculation.

Under the selected two-asset rule, both report profiles in this example have no distance-based slashing and therefore yield zero additional utility tokens. All 15 timely, valid revealers earn the same fixed per-seat ETH fee under either profile, assuming a valid ruling is issued. The modeled deviation therefore increases neither ETH fees nor additional utility-token rewards under the selected rule. Removing this particular token-reward channel does not establish truthful incentives or eliminate manipulation of the mean, the slashing band or appeal outcomes.

A public policy supplies a possible coordination focal point, but signal accuracy and limited collusion do not establish truthful best responses. Even equilibrium existence would not determine which equilibrium participants select [@kong2016peerprediction]. Claim 3 identifies a specific incentive problem in the single-asset analytical rule; the two-asset design and its interaction with appeal settlement remain open in the [blueprint's Open Questions](truth-post/blueprint/#open-questions).

This defect distinguishes exact truthful reporting from the broader objective of public benefit. Claim 3 shows why the modeled single-asset reward rule alone cannot justify a general truthful-reporting guarantee. It establishes neither net returns under the complete appeal mechanism nor effects on readers or collective decisions. A system with some strategic distortion could still improve on available alternatives; establishing that would require comparing information quality, participation costs, and downstream consequences. The present analysis establishes neither that improvement nor its absence.

Coalitions create an additional failure mode: coordinated biased reports can move the weighted mean toward the coalition's target, leaving honest reporters outside the coherence band. The simulations examine this distortion under specified reporting strategies; they do not solve for strategic best responses.

The collusion results depend on committee size, the coherence threshold $K$, honest curator noise $\sigma_{\text{honest}}$, and the reporting strategy. E2-Adv uses the predecessor mechanism with fixed-rate binary slashing and no draw-and-lock; E2' repeats the sweep with draw-and-lock, graduated slashing, and simulation-only ambiguity-driven abstention. In both 15-seat configurations at $K=1.25$, mean terminal colluder stake share is below its initial share at 0.15 and above it at 0.20. This comparison of selected grid points does not identify a breakpoint in relevance error, a safe collusion level, or a bound on profitable deviations. The noise sweep and delayed-onset experiment below examine additional dependencies under prescribed strategies.

George studies manipulation resistance in games where participants rank three or more alternatives under minimal attack-resistance assumptions [@george2023strategic]. This mechanism instead asks for scalar reports and applies a weighted-mean deviation penalty. Direct application of George's theorem would require a formal mapping between the settings; their difference alone does not establish incentive compatibility or an escape from manipulation. Claim 3 supplies a direct counterexample to truthful best response in its single-asset model; it is not a result for the two-asset mechanism or complete crowdfunded appeal payoffs.

Scalar relevance reports do not themselves establish strategyproofness. Generalized median mechanisms are strategyproof for single-peaked preferences: no voter benefits from misreporting [@moulin1980strategy]. That comparison is relevant if curators' preferences are single-peaked around their true signals, but the coherence game uses a stake-weighted mean rather than a median. An individual can move this mean through an extreme report, several times further than a median or a trimmed mean in simulated rounds; @sec-e2-prime-aggregation evaluates both alternatives and explains why the mean is kept. Where distance-based slashing applies, reports outside the graduated $K\sigma$ band can incur losses, but no claim of truthful reporting follows. Claim 3's specific reward gain applies to its single-asset model.

A coalition can also move the mean so that its members remain inside the coherence band while honest reporters fall outside it, as E2-Adv illustrates. A median would not remove this failure mode: a coalition holding a majority of the revealed weight places the median within the range of its own reports. Appeal committees may reduce distortion from chance overrepresentation when they bring more independent observations and less concentrated weights; they do not remove a pool-wide biased majority. Any additional deterrence from competitive exit depends on users recognizing degraded quality, viable alternatives, and migration reducing the attacker's expected returns. Neither scalar reporting nor the difference from George's setting establishes strategyproofness. Weighted-mean manipulation, model-dependent reward padding, and coalition coordination remain distinct risks, and the collusion sweeps do not bound all profitable deviations.

The precision assumptions for larger appeal committees are stated in [the relevance-layer description](#relevance-layer). They do not determine whether a deviation improves expected scalar appeal payouts or remains profitable after the full settlement process. The public crowdfunding rule requires the additional choices in [Public appeal funding](#sec-appeal-funding). Whether escalation raises the colluding stake needed for a given amount of distortion remains open because escalation dynamics are not simulated here. A possible refinement is to ask curators to predict dispersion and score that prediction with a proper scoring rule; whether this separates informed agreement from lazy convergence or resists collusion remains untested.

The specified stake-based mechanism does not prevent an actor from acquiring majority influence. Acquisition costs depend on market depth, existing holdings, and the means of obtaining stake. Buying a large platform-token position into limited liquidity can incur increasing slippage and produce observable market activity, but superlinear cost and timely detection are not guaranteed. Depreciation could deter capture if the token's value depends on the affected pool, users recognize degraded curation and migrate, and the attacker's expected loss exceeds the external benefit of capture. Its strength depends on the dedicated utility token's external uses and market; ETH service fees and appeal funding do not establish the acquisition cost or capture resistance of utility-token staking.

Separate pool accounting prevents one pool's adjudication from automatically changing another pool's state. It does not guarantee independent security when pools share curators, capital, dispute providers, or interfaces, nor does permissionless creation ensure that a funded migration destination exists. Externally motivated attackers may accept losses as an operational expense. The present design provides no general resolution of majority-stake capture; stronger defenses would require additional mechanisms and assumptions beyond those evaluated here.

## Participation conditions

The system requires authors, challengers, and curators. Each faces a participation decision against an outside option of doing nothing.

**Claim 4.** *Sustained voluntary participation requires each role's expected return to cover its outside option. The following are candidate participation conditions, not sufficient conditions for equilibrium existence:*

*(i) Author entry: the value honest authors assign to expected confidence, reputation and external benefits covers publication effort and the opportunity cost of bonded capital.*

*(ii) Challenger entry: search has non-negative expected value at the challenger's costs and available rewards, as in Claim 2.*

*(iii) Curator entry: expected service fees, token rewards and other benefits, net of expected token losses and assessment costs, cover the opportunity cost of committed capital. Comparing the two assets requires an explicit valuation; raw token and ETH quantities cannot be added.*

*These conditions are interdependent: entry changes detection, reward competition, stake distribution, and funding demand. Checking them separately does not establish mutually consistent best responses or dynamic stability.*

Challenger exit could allow false claims to accumulate and renew incentives to search, but no entry-exit dynamics are simulated here. Journalistic reputation, ideological commitment, or interface-level bounties may change participation incentives; they do not supply an established bound on this risk. Claim 3 further prevents inferring truthful equilibrium from positive participation returns.

# Related Work

This work sits at the intersection of information quality, dispute systems, and cryptoeconomic coordination.

**Data quality.** Wang and Strong's multidimensional treatment of data quality is the main conceptual anchor for the quality-identification step [@wang1996beyondaccuracy]. The methodological lesson adopted here is to identify the relevant quality dimensions before choosing mechanisms.

**Falsifiability.** Popper motivates exposing claims to potential empirical refutation [@popper1959logic, secs. 6, 15]. His logical asymmetry does not establish a cost advantage for challenging bounded news claims; the mechanism requires that separate economic condition.

**Schelling-style coordination and decentralized courts.** Buterin's SchellingCoin proposal describes an early cryptoeconomic oracle built on Schelling-point coordination: participants commit to and then reveal a value, and those whose values fall between the 25th and 75th percentiles are paid, on the premise that the truth is "arguably the most powerful Schelling point" [@buterin2014schellingcoin]. The proposal grants that a majority coalition sets the median and that a 49% coalition likely can break the scheme. It also considers a 1% entity that announces a false value and pays a nominal reward to those who report it, but judges that such an entity would fail in practice because unseating the dominant focal point is a massive coordination problem. The $p+\varepsilon$ attack, conceived by Andrew Miller and described by Buterin, needs no such coordination: a briber who credibly commits to pay each reporter of the false value the reward $p$ for matching the majority plus a margin $\varepsilon$, if that value loses, makes the false report a dominant strategy and pays nothing when the attack succeeds [@buterin2015pepsilon]. Kleros and related systems carry the pattern into decentralized adjudication, showing how stake, commit-reveal, and appeals can implement it [@kleros2019shortpaper; @kleros2024yellowpaper]. The modeled Truth Post design assumes Kleros v1 as the external DDR provider, with the challenge manager implementing the `IArbitrable` interface. The mechanism is a deliberate Keynesian beauty contest: participants coordinate on expected consensus rather than on truth directly [@bergolla2022kleros; @kleros2021cryptoeconomics]. This structure is intended to aggregate information by anchoring coordination to a substantive standard: in Kleros, the legally correct answer is the intended focal point. The coherence game in this paper adopts that design intention, substituting a public curation policy for the legal standard. An arbitrary or self-referential focal point can undermine this aim; a public standard alone does not establish informed reporting or equilibrium selection [@schelling1960strategy; @rojoarjona2021focalpoints; @george2023strategic]. George and Lesaege catalogue concrete $p+\varepsilon$ attack variants on Schelling-game-based systems [@george2021ppsilon], and George separately analyzes griefing factors that arise in Schelling-based mechanisms [@george2023griefing]. Ast et al. survey the state of decentralized justice more broadly, cataloguing recurring criticisms and next-generation research directions [@ast2023decentralized]. Random drafting makes advance identification of committee members harder, but does not prevent bribes conditional on selection. Graduated slashing can increase the cost of deviations that incur a penalty; a coherent coalition may avoid that penalty. Neither feature removes the coordination risk.

**Oracle and dispute prior art.** Reality.eth and UMA demonstrate optimistic, escalation-based dispute flows for on-chain questions [@realityeth2023; @umaOptimisticOracleDocs; @umaWhitepaperRepo]. Their importance here is not that they solve curation, but that they demonstrate dispute resolution patterns the accuracy layer can reuse.

**Token-curated registries (TCRs).** TCRs propose coordinating on list membership through stake, challenge, and voting primitives [@goldin2017tcr]. The closest formal game-theoretic analysis of this class derives challenge-occurrence conditions and identifies multi-equilibrium regions [@asgaonkar2018tcrgame]; the incentive analysis here addresses related participation questions, but under a mechanism that separates accuracy from relevance rather than compressing admission into one vote. Deployed TCRs exhibit engagement failures, for which Wang and Krishnamachari propose a token-inflation remedy [@wang2018tcrinflation]. Truth Post's bootstrap failure is architecturally different (disputes route to Kleros, not to a native token electorate) but sits in the same failure family.

**TCR variants and related constructions.** Ito and Tanaka use PageRank over a citation graph as a centrality-based alternative to random curator assignment [@ito2019tcrcitation]; stake-weighted random drafting avoids the pre-existing-topology requirement at the cost of weaker competence targeting. Kosmarski and Gordiychuk apply TCRs to scholarly journal curation [@kosmarski2020tcrjournal]; their instantiation retains the single-dimension compression Truth Post avoids, but the pattern of repurposing TCRs for an editorial context is the nearest prior art. Crites, Maller, Meiklejohn, and Mercer give the first provably secure TCR construction with cryptographic vote privacy [@crites2020reputable]; "trustless" here is cryptoeconomic (no single operational point of control, bonded incentives, decentralized dispute resolution), not the cryptographic-secrecy sense their construction targets. Truth Post differs from the TCR line overall by treating the unit as claims plus evidence plus disputes, and by separating accuracy from relevance instead of compressing everything into one registry.

**Peer prediction and decentralized peer review.** Peer-prediction schemes seek to elicit informative reports under assumptions about signals and beliefs, using payments contingent on others' reports [@miller2005peerprediction; @prelec2004bts]. The commit-reveal coherence game here shares the same incentive pattern but anchors the focal point to a public policy document rather than to eliciting beliefs. Beyond news, a systematic survey of blockchain-based peer review [@favaro2024peerreview] and a recent open-science peer-review mechanism [@finke2024peerreview] use an adjacent family of primitives (remuneration, disclosure, reputation, certificates). Their domain differs from news, but their decomposition into separable quality dimensions is consistent with the framework used here.

**Prediction markets and governance.** Prediction markets and futarchy are related attempts to aggregate dispersed information [@hanson2013futarchy]. They differ in operating cost and question structure. This paper does not use continuous trading markets because the target domains involve high-dimensional claim spaces and semantic disputes rather than a small number of liquid future-event questions.

**Public inquiry and commons governance.** Dewey treats public discussion as a source of knowledge about social needs, while Ostrom studies arrangements through which users participate in rules and hold monitors accountable [@dewey1927public, pp. 206–209; @ostrom1990commons, pp. 90, 93–94]. These works expose requirements that open access to protocol transactions alone does not meet. The architectural tradeoff is discussed above; the implications for pool policy and public benefit are developed below.

# Threat Model

The protocol assumes adversaries can be rational, coordinated, well-funded, and persistent. The table below summarizes the principal attacks and their design responses; the paragraphs that follow explain each response's intended effect and limitations.

| Attack | Design response |
|---|---|
| False claims survive because challenging is uneconomic | Bonded publication plus debunking rewards |
| Colluding curators try to bend relevance | Drafted committees, draw-and-lock with graduated slashing, relevance-round escalation |
| Non-falsifiable or vague claims exploit semantic ambiguity | Structured claim templates plus `NonFalsifiable` challenge reason |
| Off-topic claims pollute a pool | `ScopeViolation` challenge reason for topic mismatch |
| Claims bypass template rules via direct contract interaction | On-chain structural validation at submission; `TemplateViolation` challenge reason for semantic non-conformance |
| Bad pools set degenerate policies or parameters | Permissionless competition plus interface filtering rather than governance veto |
| A dominant frontend recentralizes discovery | Canonical protocol state and replaceable interfaces |
| Reputation creates unbonded influence | No reputation-weighted curation mechanism exists; author reputation is a separate standing bond only |
| Low-participation pools fail to bootstrap | Pool creators seed local reward budgets; interfaces can ignore inactive pools |
| Stale claims linger forever | Confidence only accumulates while bonded; withdrawn claims remain historical rather than active |
| Permissionless publishing surfaces harmful or illegal content | Protocol is content-neutral; interfaces filter according to local norms and legal requirements |
| An ideological pool curates biased content under a permissive policy | Each bonded claim remains challengeable under its pool's evidence policy; biased relevance may motivate competitive exit |
| Curators converge on conventional wisdom, suppressing nuanced truth | Utility-token penalties and appeals are proposed mitigations; truthful reporting is not established |

**False-claim survival.** Bonded publication forces the author to lock capital that a successful challenger captures. Claim 1 derives the bond threshold $B^*$ above which false publication has negative expected value in its reduced-form model; E1 evaluates conditional challenger returns and survival across selected parameters. The deterrence calculation depends on detection coverage and adjudication accuracy rather than a fixed bond multiple.

**Curator collusion.** A colluding bloc that coordinates scores can shift the weighted mean and slash honest reporters who fall outside the coherence band. Commit-reveal prevents copying unrevealed votes, and draw-and-lock makes committee membership uncertain in advance. Bribes conditional on selection remain possible, and graduated slashing increases deviation costs only when it imposes a penalty. Claim 3 separates this coalition risk from individual incentive compatibility. A weighted median or trimmed mean would not remove it (@sec-e2-prime-aggregation). E2-Adv and @sec-e2-prime show increasing distortion across the tested colluding fractions; they do not establish a safe fraction or a breakpoint in error.

**Non-falsifiable claims.** A vague or unfalsifiable claim is harder to catch through binary `Debunking` adjudication because jurors have weaker grounds to rule against a proposition that is not clearly false, only ill-posed. The `NonFalsifiable` challenge reason routes such claims to adjudication on falsifiability rather than truth, where the question is whether the proposition meets the pool's template and evidence-policy requirements. E3 quantifies the retention-cost reduction as a function of prevalence and the adjudication-accuracy gap between dedicated falsifiability review and forced-binary truth adjudication.

**Off-topic claims.** A claim may be well-formed and factually defensible but belong to the wrong topic domain. The `ScopeViolation` challenge reason lets any participant flag domain mismatch post-publication, routing adjudication to the question of whether the claim falls within the pool's declared scope rather than whether it is true.

**Template-violating claims.** On-chain structural validation at submission enforces minimal field presence (non-empty CIDs, valid version pointers), but a claim can pass those checks while still violating the pool's semantic template requirements: disallowed source classes, missing required evidence fields, or incorrect formatting. The `TemplateViolation` challenge reason enforces these semantic constraints post-publication without requiring computationally expensive on-chain content analysis at submission time.

**Bad pools.** Permissionless pool creation means degenerate policies cannot be prevented at the protocol level. Trivial relevance policies may produce undifferentiated scores, and adversarial templates may discourage authors from publishing. Competitive correction requires users to recognize quality differences, funded alternatives to exist, and authors, curators, and sponsors to coordinate migration. Interface filtering may reduce exposure, but neither response guarantees that bad pools disappear.

**Frontend recentralization.** An interface cannot change canonical on-chain state, but it can omit records or display false outputs. Public state makes independent verification and competing interfaces possible; it does not ensure that readers verify displays or discover alternatives. Effective competition still requires usable indexing, distribution, and reader adoption.

**Reputation as unbonded influence.** An earlier design allowed accumulated curator reputation to increase curation weight, granting influence not backed by slashable capital. The current design eliminates reputation-weighted curation entirely. Drafting and voting are purely stake-driven: influence requires locking capital at risk, and there is no mechanism through which historical performance translates into unslashable voting power.

**Bootstrap failure.** A new pool needs authors, challengers, curators, and a reward budget. Pool creators seed local reward budgets to attract curators, and bonded claims remain challengeable before relevance rounds run. Claim 4 identifies interdependent participation requirements; it does not establish equilibrium or stable entry dynamics.

**Stale claims.** Confidence keeps accumulating while a claim remains bonded and `Live`. Capital opportunity cost may encourage withdrawal, and new evidence can support a challenge. But subsequent events need not falsify a time-scoped historical claim: it can remain accurate while losing relevance. Bond-time does not measure freshness and can favor older claims. Relevance updates and interface ranking must address this distinction; withdrawal alone is not an established remedy.

**Harmful content.** The protocol does not perform content moderation because it has no content-level semantics: canonical state records bonds, challenges, and scores, not rendered text. Interfaces, which do render content, filter according to their own policies and local legal requirements. This is the same separation that operates in other permissionless systems: the transport layer is neutral, and the application layer applies editorial judgment. The limitation is that the defense depends on interface-level action; a negligent or complicit interface can surface harmful content without violating any protocol rule.

**Ideological echo chambers.** A pool whose policy favors a viewpoint can reward agreement around biased relevance judgments. Even faithful policy enforcement would preserve that bias. Any bonded claim remains challengeable under its pool's evidence policy, but adjudication is pool-specific; common DDR access does not guarantee that different policies yield the same outcome. Relevance scores are local to the pool, while their effects on readers and public decisions need not be. User exit is a proposed defense whose informational and funding preconditions are discussed below.

**Lazy-consensus convergence.** The coherence game rewards agreement with the terminal adjudicated mean, which can reward convergence on conventional wisdom even when the crowd is systematically wrong. This is distinct from active collusion: curators can independently anchor on a lazy prior. A low-dispersion committee is penalized only when an appeal moves the terminal adjudicated score outside its band. Without an appeal, reports near the committee's own mean are coherent, and no distance-based penalty means no additional utility-token reward. This treats unchallenged lazy consensus and informed agreement alike; both earn the same fixed ETH fee per timely, validly revealed seat when a valid ruling is issued. Claim 3 demonstrates artificial-dispersion rewards only in its single-asset analytical model. Appeals may discipline sufficiently large errors when the appeal committee brings additional independent information. They do not guarantee truthful best responses, and a uniformly biased pool can produce the same bias in larger committees.

Several threats remain partially unresolved: off-chain collusion, legal pressure against visible participants, pool-policy degeneracy, coordinated capture above a sufficiently large colluding bloc, lazy-consensus convergence when the crowd is systematically wrong, and free-rider extraction of canonical on-chain state by third-party aggregators.

# Evaluation

Evaluating the central thesis requires testing both whether private incentives induce productive curation and whether its outputs benefit affected people. This suite examines components of that pathway through a conditional viability analysis. It measures outcomes under stipulated strategies and selected parameter settings, rather than predicting where a live deployment will land. The behavioral parameters are not empirically calibrated; the reported sweeps vary selected inputs while others remain fixed. The results identify configurations with favorable modeled challenger returns, relevance errors, or stake trajectories. They do not prove that the stipulated strategies are best responses, that truthful reporting is an equilibrium, or that a deployment will occupy those configurations.

Routine activity logs alone would not identify the behavioral parameters. Estimating $p_{\text{detect}}$ requires an independently examined sample that includes unchallenged claims. Estimating $p_{\text{juror}}$ requires reference assessments independent of the court's own outcomes. Estimating $\sigma_{\text{honest}}$ requires benchmark tasks and an explicit model separating signal error from bias, strategic reports, and legitimate policy disagreement. Each reference assessment carries uncertainty that calibration must report.

The suite focuses on four questions:

- When is it economically rational to challenge false claims?
- How robust is drafted-curator relevance curation to noise and collusion?
- What follows if a dedicated `NonFalsifiable` challenge reason materially improves adjudication accuracy on otherwise non-falsifiable claims?
- How do reputation stocks separate under prescribed outcome probabilities, and how does pool scoping affect cross-pool carryover?

| Parameter | Value | Role | Source | Calibration status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p_{\text{juror}}$ | 0.80 (E1 sweep 0.50--0.99) | Per-juror accuracy in DDR panels | Assumed | Unvalidated; swept |
| $p_{\text{detect}}$ | 0.35 anchor (swept 0.05--0.80) | Probability a false claim is discovered and challenged | Illustrative anchor | Unvalidated; swept |
| $K$ | 1.25 baseline; E2/E2' sweep 0.8, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5 | Coherence-band multiplier ($K\sigma$) | Reference parameter | Unvalidated; swept |
| $\sigma_{\text{honest}}$ | 0.08 (swept 0.05--0.20) | Standard deviation of honest signal noise before clipping | Assumed moderate noise | Unvalidated; swept |
| $\delta$ | 0.01/round | Author reputation decay rate | Assumed | Unvalidated; fixed |
| $f$ | 0.25 | Non-falsifiable share of adjudicated bad items (E3 only) | Assumed | Unvalidated; scenario input |
| $p_{\text{nf}}$ | 0.85 | Juror accuracy on NonFalsifiable challenges (E3 only) | Assumed | Unvalidated; scenario input |
| $N$ | 5 | Jurors per modeled dispute panel | Assumed | Fixed scenario input |

Stochastic experiments use 100 Monte Carlo seeds, except E4d, which uses 200; the single-round aggregation-rule comparison in @tbl-e2-prime-aggregation draws independent rounds instead. Reported 95% confidence intervals quantify sampling variation conditional on the model, not uncertainty in its assumptions. E3 and the E1 detection-sensitivity sweep are closed-form calculations. {#tbl-param-assumptions}

These runs have not been rerun with the current 80% drawn-weight quorum and do not establish that rule's availability or adversarial robustness.
